ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Progress Note 4 — Sick Visit — Mary McLeod Bethune — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Same-day sick visit for an asthma exacerbation with a cold

text.paragraph: Worsening wheeze and breathlessness for two days with a cold. [S]

Mrs. Bethune called the clinic this morning from the yellow zone of her action plan and was seen the same day. Five days ago she developed a cold with a runny nose and sore throat after a crowded church gathering. For two days her wheeze and chest tightness have worsened; she woke three times last night and has needed eight extra inhalations of budesonide-formoterol in each of the last two days, as her plan allows. Her morning peak flow has fallen from about 300 to 210 L/min. She can speak in full sentences and has no chest pain. She has no fever, green sputum or leg swelling, and has had no ankle swelling or orthopnea that would suggest heart failure. She takes her maintenance inhalations with the spacer, amlodipine and atorvastatin as prescribed. She has never been admitted to hospital for asthma or needed a breathing tube. [S]

text.paragraph: Vital signs recorded on 1948-06-15; see the Vital Signs section. [S]

tr.td: Alert, sitting upright, speaking in full sentences; not using accessory muscles
Pulse 98, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air, temperature 37.4 °C; peak flow 205 L/min (60 percent of her best)
Head, eyes, ears, nose, and throat
Widespread expiratory wheeze with good air entry; no crackles
Regular rhythm; jugular venous pressure not raised; no edema
After albuterol 8 puffs by spacer three times over an hour: peak flow 275 L/min (81 percent), oxygen saturation 96 percent, pulse 92, wheeze much reduced

Wheeze, cough and breathlessness for four months: waking with cough and tight chest two or three nights a week, breathless on one flight of stairs, relieved by albuterol, worse with colds, dust and strong scents; known asthma for many years but never confirmed by lung function testing and never treated with an inhaled steroid. Asthma, COPD and heart failure to be distinguished: spirometry with bronchodilator response, FeNO and an echocardiogram booked
S — Synthetic presenting problem anchored to her documented chronic asthma. Superseded by the diagnosis at the second visit.
Blocked nose, thick postnasal drip and a reduced sense of smell for years, worse in the last year; no nosebleeds; never seen by an ear, nose and throat specialist
S — Synthetic upper-airway symptoms; superseded by the diagnosis of chronic rhinosinusitis after nasal endoscopy.
Gastro-esophageal reflux: heartburn and an acid taste two or three evenings a week, worse after late meals and lying down; no trouble swallowing, vomiting, black stools or weight loss
S — Synthetic comorbidity of asthma; not a claim about her real health.
Obesity, class 1 (BMI 33.1); she wants to walk more and to keep up with her work, and agreed to talk about it
S — Synthetic comorbidity recorded in her words and with her agreement; not a claim about her real weight.

Moderate asthma exacerbation triggered by a cold: two days of worsening wheeze and night waking despite eight reliever inhalations a day, peak flow 205 L/min (60 percent of her best), oxygen saturation 94 percent; improved to 275 L/min in clinic; treated without admission; resolved
S — Synthetic exacerbation; not a claim about a real attack.

Asthma, confirmed: variable airflow obstruction (FEV1 64 percent predicted, rising 270 mL or 21 percent after bronchodilator, with a normal post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC of 0.72 and normal DLCO); type 2 inflammation (FeNO 46 ppb, blood eosinophils 0.42 x10^3/uL, total IgE 210, house dust mite sensitization); not COPD and not heart failure. Uncontrolled at diagnosis on albuterol alone
S — Synthetic modern confirmation linked to her documented chronic asthma.

Hypertensive heart disease without heart failure: clinic blood pressure 152/88 and 146/86, home average 144/84; mild concentric left ventricular hypertrophy with grade 1 diastolic dysfunction and a normal ejection fraction (62 percent); BNP 48 pg/mL
S — Synthetic finding of the modern work-up; not a claim about her real heart.
Hyperlipidemia: LDL cholesterol 144 mg/dL; 10-year ASCVD risk above 20 percent with hypertension
Chronic rhinosinusitis without nasal polyps: years of congestion, postnasal drip and reduced smell, with mucosal swelling and mucus in both middle meatuses and no polyps on nasal endoscopy
S — Synthetic upper-airway comorbidity of asthma; not a claim about her real health.

list.item:
Moderate asthma exacerbation triggered by a cold (J45.41). A moderate exacerbation: peak flow 60 percent of her best, saturation 94 percent, speaking in full sentences, with a good response in clinic. Heart failure is unlikely: no orthopnea or edema and a normal jugular venous pressure, with normal pumping function and no raised filling pressures on the echocardiogram three months ago. Safe to go home with treatment and close follow-up; no antibiotic, because there are no signs of bacterial infection. [S]
Prednisone 40 mg each morning for five days.
Budesonide-formoterol maintenance increased to two inhalations twice daily, with one as needed, up to 12 a day in total.
Peak flow morning and evening; go to the emergency department or call 911 if peak flow falls below 170, she cannot speak in sentences, or her lips turn blue.
Nurse telephone calls in two and seven days; review in clinic within a week.

Asthma (J45.40). First exacerbation needing an oral corticosteroid since she started ICS-formoterol; a cold was the trigger. [S]
Action plan reviewed with her; it worked as intended.
Influenza, COVID-19 and RSV vaccines in the autumn.

Hypertensive heart disease (I11.9). Blood pressure 138/82 while unwell on albuterol. [S]
Continue amlodipine.

text.paragraph: Guideline basis: Global Strategy for Asthma Management and Prevention, 2025 update (2025); 2020 Focused Updates to the Asthma Management Guidelines: A Report from the National Asthma Education and Prevention Program Coordinating Committee Expert Panel Working Group (2020)

Follow-up: Nurse telephone calls in two and seven days. Clinic review within a week. Emergency care for any red-zone sign. Next scheduled visit 1948-07-27: review six weeks after an exacerbation: control, repeat spirometry and FeNO, biologic assessment, blood pressure and the post-exacerbation plan. [S]
